taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; Texas is within the native range. Historical laxa names are synonymized.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Dalea frutescens as native in Texas.
Hays County — University of Texas Purola Preserve flora lists Dalea frutescens among plants occurring naturally rather than introduced.
Kerr County — Barneby's Dalea monograph explicitly discusses Kerr County material and the species as common on the Edwards Plateau.
Val Verde County — Barneby documents the type of the synonym Parosela laxa from Devils River, Val Verde County, within the current D. frutescens concept.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Cultivated pollinator-garden records are not counted toward the three-county threshold; the decision uses natural/herbarium/floristic evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: First decide whether the plant is woody: D. frutescens is the low intricately branched shrub in this batch, with many tiny leaflets on pale gray/straw branchlets and short terminal flower spikes.
diagnostic_traits: low woody shrub/subshrub, usually under about 1 m, intricately branched
older stems pale brown and furrowed; younger twigs greenish to gray/straw and glandular
odd-pinnate leaves with usually 4–9 pairs of tiny obovate to oblanceolate leaflets plus a terminal leaflet
leaflets brighter above, paler and gland-punctate beneath
terminal or leaf-opposed short spikes, usually subcapitate to moderately dense
calyx short-toothed and glossy/glabrous externally, but silky-ciliate around the mouth
flower sessile; bicolored petals are a supporting cue rather than the primary identifier

confusers.separator: D. frutescens has a short-toothed shiny calyx that is nearly hairless outside and silky mainly around the mouth; D. formosa is separated by its conspicuously plumose/feathery calyx-lobe treatment.
D. aurea is an herbaceous perennial with a fuzzy dense head and only a few larger silky leaflets; D. frutescens is woody and many-leafleted.
D. compacta is herbaceous with linear leaflets and a dense terminal head; D. frutescens remains visibly woody and intricately branched.
